General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism
The capital attracted migrants from all these groups, especially people who came in search of work and a living.
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism
This gives us another possible source of the ideological direction we have already identified within Sufism.
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism
We can see the effect of this social background even more clearly when we add the widespread poverty found in these same environments and the large number of Sufis among the poor.
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism
The historian al-Muqaddasī, who died in 350 AH/961 CE, tells us that during a visit to Shiraz he wanted to learn about the local Sufi way of life.
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism
He made contact with the Sufis there.
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism
When he received gifts of clothing and purses of money, he would take them and then give them to the Sufis.
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism
This clearly suggests that he saw they needed such things because they were poor.
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism
Poverty, in fact, followed the Sufis in almost every part of that society.
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism
But their poverty was not caused by Sufism.
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism
The opposite is closer to the truth.
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism
Poverty was not the result of Sufism. It was one of the conditions that helped produce it.
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism
Poverty was a social phenomenon affecting many lower and middle groups throughout different regions and environments.
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism

So it is not enough to say that the Sufis were poor because they freely chose a life of asceticism and hardship in order to escape the “evils” of the world and the “impurity” of matter, whether for religious or philosophical reasons.
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism
That explanation may apply to a small group, or to a few individuals.
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism
It does not explain the great majority who formed the wider social phenomenon.
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism
History tells us that during the third and fourth Islamic centuries—the ninth and tenth centuries CE—the urban masses experienced serious social unrest.
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism
These masses included artisans, street sellers, owners of small shops, people living in extreme poverty, and the unemployed.
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism
As their living conditions deteriorated, these groups formed organizations of their own.
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism
Within each trade or group, these organizations had a cooperative side.
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism
At the same time, they could also take violent action against the authorities, wealthy merchants, and large landowners.
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism
Among them were groups known at the time as the ʿayyārūn and shuṭṭār.
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism
They attracted people from many sections of society who were angry at class inequality because they suffered some of the harshest forms of poverty.
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism
Their members came from different ethnic backgrounds without racial distinction among them.
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism
Historians of the period give vivid descriptions of the decline in social conditions affecting these groups.
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism
One example is al-Muqaddasī’s description of Iraq at the time:
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism
“It is the home of disorder and high prices. Every day it falls further behind, and injustice and taxation keep it in hardship and misery.”
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism

What matters for us here is the possible connection between these social conditions and another well-established historical fact: Sufi activity became especially intense during the same period in which these problems became severe.
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism
We are not alone in seeing such a connection.
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism
A leading modern Arab scholar writes that “these conditions may have had an effect on the growth of Sufi activity.”
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism
In reality, the strong growth of Sufism during this period can be seen as another form of the social groupings we have just described.
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism
It brought together one section of the destitute poor.
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism
What united them, besides poverty, may have been an intellectual bond, or perhaps a personal tendency toward dependence and withdrawal from the exhausting struggle to earn a living.
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism
Historical sources give us several pictures of these gatherings of the “poor.”
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism

They describe people who longed intensely for good food and, when it became available without effort, threw themselves upon it with something close to greed—or perhaps with actual greed produced by deprivation.
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism
Abū al-ʿAlāʾ al-Maʿarrī was therefore not simply inventing a fantasy when he mocked the Sufis’ enthusiasm for food:
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism
I see the Sufi clan as the worst of clans. So tell them—and how little such men deserve: Did God say, when you worshipped Him, “Eat like cattle, and dance for Me”?
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism
Nor was it without a real basis that “the eating of the Sufis” became proverbial at the time.
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism

Indeed, one of the leading Sufi authorities confirms that reality in a story told about him. It is said that he acquired loads of white sugar and called together a group of confectioners, until they built from the sugar a wall with battlements and prayer niches supported by columns, all of it carved from sugar. Then he invited the Sufis, who tore it down, smashed it apart, and carried it off.
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism

There were other features of Sufism in the third and fourth centuries AH that strengthen our view that its spread at the time was partly a form of social dislocation caused by widespread poverty, unemployment, and deprivation. These included the spread of sexual deviance among their ranks, as well as the practice known as kaldiyya. The fact that leading Sufi writers strongly condemned these practices and called for Sufism to be cleansed of them only confirms that they existed. It does not prove the opposite.
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism

What we want to show from this historical survey is that the decisive factor behind the growth of Sufism in this period was the social reality itself, not the conscious choices of individuals. From this, we can also trace the ideological direction of the Sufi movement back to its real social basis, independently of what the Sufis themselves consciously intended.
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism

We are not claiming that the Sufis alone represented the outlook of all the broad and varied groups in their society who suffered under the class oppression and tyranny of the existing social order. But we do argue that the Sufis were the only ones who raised the ideological content of their movement to a theoretical level. At that level, it could stand face to face with the ideology through which the ruling system influenced and controlled society as a whole. That influence even reached the social groups whose material and spiritual misery had been caused by this “official” ideology—in fact, it reached those groups most of all.
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism
With this social basis established, we can now turn to the second side of our discussion of the persecution of the Sufis: how the different groups in society responded to the Sufi movement in Islam.
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism

B — The Attitude of the Ruling System: It should now be easy to understand why the despotic caliphate used persecution against the Sufi movement. In fact, we may not need much more explanation. What we do need is to give some examples of this persecution, because they support the central point of our study: that the Sufi form taken by Arab-Islamic philosophy, alongside its other, rationalist form, was in its essential content one expression of the ideological struggles of the Middle Ages.
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism

If the Sufi movement had not carried this kind of content, it would not have been “subjected to attack and retaliation.” There is no solid basis for explaining its persecution as the result of purely religious motives.
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism

Medieval Islamic history is full of blatant violations of Islamic law and teaching by the Abbasid caliphs in particular, as well as by the people around them. Why, then, did religious feeling fail to prevent these violations? Why did the jurists not act as defenders of religion by condemning them, or by stirring up the public against those responsible, as they did especially against the Sufi philosophers? And why did “the Sunnis unanimously reject Sufism,” when Sunni doctrine was almost always the religious and ideological foundation of Abbasid rule, apart from the period of al-Maʾmūn?
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism
Claude Cahen points us toward the answer: “Islam rarely behaves intolerantly in cases where politics is not involved.”
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism
In reality, the ideological position of the Sufi movement did not always remain confined to philosophy. At times, it became practical action.
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism
“In the year 200 AH, a group appeared in Alexandria who were called Sufis. They commanded what was right and forbade what was wrong, and they opposed the ruler in his actions…”
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism

“Those in power during the Abbasid period, as well as the followers of official Sunnism, had little sympathy for these Sufis, who showed contempt for high rank and condemned the moral corruption of members of the court. But the people in general respected them, because they criticized the rich and listened to the complaints of the destitute (…)”
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism
“The conditions prevailing in the country were turning people’s attention toward Sufism.”
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism

“The Sufis were not content simply to give human feelings a divine character. They also wanted to give human will this same divine character, and on that basis they claimed that this supposedly divine will possessed divine power over everything. Through doctrines of this kind, they posed the greatest dangers to the peace and stability of the state. Around 300 AH/912 CE, the number of people accused of heresy increased noticeably. Then, in 309 AH/921 CE, al-Ḥusayn ibn Manṣūr al-Ḥallāj was put to death in a horrific manner. He was given a thousand lashes, his hands and feet were cut off, and he was burned…”
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism
The influence of the Sufis also meant that:
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism

“The way people understood the ideal Islamic life began to change. They came to see it from a perspective different from the one approved by the teachings of the Sunni schools. The Sufis therefore had a powerful influence on the masses who came under their sway, and people’s admiration for the military character of the heroes of Islam began to decline. As a result, toward the end of the ninth century CE, when an intolerant Sunni spirit became dominant in Baghdad, many prominent Sufis were hunted down and persecuted in a manner resembling the Inquisition.”
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism
There is further evidence that, among its best and most principled figures, Sufism could represent a revolt against unjust rulers and the exploiting class:
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism

“Hārūn al-Rashīd was once walking with his attendants, servants, and slaves ahead of him when a Sufi shouted: ‘Hārūn! You have exhausted both the people and the animals.’ Another Sufi told him: ‘Every other person is responsible for himself, but you are responsible for everyone.’ The Sufis used many different ways to rebuke rulers and call them to account (…) Politicians tried to buy the Sufis’ religion and their consciences, offering whatever price was necessary to make them keep silent about injustice and corruption. The sincere refused. The professionals accepted.”
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism

For all these reasons, it has been said that Sufi teachings, “in their popular form, brought together great numbers of Muslims,” and that “people became attached to the Sufis and sought their blessing.”
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism

This also explains why the vizier Abū Ḥāmid feared the anger of the public after al-Ḥallāj’s trial. He tried to distance himself from responsibility for the execution and spread that responsibility among everyone involved. He gathered the witnesses and jurists who had approved the sentence and instructed them to assemble around the place where al-Ḥallāj had been crucified and all cry out together:
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism
“Yes! Kill him! His death is for the good of the Muslims!”
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism
These, then, were the two sides: the attitude of the authorities toward the Sufis, and the attitude of the masses from the lower and middle social groups.
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism

At their real social level, both positions arose from class interests, whether the people involved were conscious of this or not. The class dimension is an objective reality. It does not stop being real simply because people lack class consciousness.
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism

The class that holds economic and political power, however, usually has a highly developed sense of its own class interests. Because it controls the means of power and domination, it not only protects its own class ideology but also tries to impose that ideology on the opposing class. At times, the oppressed can even become more zealous in defending that ideology than the people who produced it in the first place.
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism

Yet in the case we are discussing, the ordinary people seem to have possessed something we might call a class “instinct” toward a social order that relentlessly oppressed and impoverished them. Perhaps it was this class instinct that allowed them to recognize which side to support in the conflict between the authorities and the Sufis.
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism

Their support, however, had little effect because it remained limited in scale. We can explain this weakness through two factors. First, the ordinary population remained economically, socially, and culturally underdeveloped. Second, Sufi thought itself was unable to give its ideological content a realistic form that could actually be put into practice. It therefore could not become a full expression of the ideology of those masses within the historical conditions of the time.
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism
One question remains: the attitude of the conservative jurists toward the Sufis.
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism

We have already touched on this during our discussion. In our view, the jurists followed the authorities and supported their ideology. Their position was not an independent one genuinely driven by a desire to preserve the beliefs of Islam and defend the sharia, as they themselves claimed and as later scholars often explain it.
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism

This is why some researchers, especially modern ones, place the persecution of the Sufis on the wrong historical ground. They reduce the issue to a struggle between jurists and Sufis. One explanation describes the jurists’ hostility to the Sufis as something that:
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism

“did not appear until the Sufis had organized themselves into groups and communities, disciples had gathered around their shaykhs, and ordinary people had begun to flock to these circles. People started drinking from the spring of Sufi sainthood and seeking blessings from the great Sufi masters. The Sufis therefore became the focus of public attention and took a leading place among Muslims as a whole. Before this, it had been the jurists who held this position in Muslim society (…) The jurists consequently became resentful of the Sufis. They began accusing them of wrongdoing, plotting against them, and circulating their sayings and ecstatic utterances in ways that made them appear to be unbelievers who had strayed from the faith. This then made it lawful to kill them, burn them, and drive them from their homes.”
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism
Under this explanation, a tragic historical conflict becomes little more than a personal rivalry between two groups competing for leadership by trying to attract the ordinary population.
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism

To shift the issue away from its real social basis in this way is, in the end, to strip the Sufi movement—and Sufi thought in particular—of its ideological content. We cannot say whether this interpretation is deliberate and follows from a particular ideology, or whether it simply comes from a shallow understanding of the issue.
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism
The tragedy of the Sufis in medieval Islamic history deserves a much deeper explanation, grounded in the historical conditions of the time.
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism

And this interpretation does something else that takes us just as far from reality. Just as it strips Sufi thought of its revolutionary content, it also strips the ordinary people’s support for the Sufis of its revolutionary social meaning. Their position is turned into a purely religious one, supposedly driven by a desire “to drink from the spring of Sufi sainthood and seek blessings from the great Sufi masters.”
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism

As though these people had no other problems. As though nothing else occupied their lives or demanded their attention except deciding where to drink from the spiritual spring and where to seek “religious blessings”: from the jurists, or from the Sufis!
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism
Finally, we should make clear that our study of Islamic Sufism, and the conclusions we have drawn from it, concern Sufism mainly in its philosophical form.
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism

This means that our study is limited to the periods when Sufism was an intellectual activity built on certain theoretical foundations. Those foundations had an ideological direction that we have identified at several points in this study. This is why we have been justified in treating Sufism as one form of Arab-Islamic philosophical thought in the Middle Ages, though one with its own distinctive character and its own theory.
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism

But Sufism also had another side: practical conduct and a particular way of life. During the periods we have been studying, this practical side existed alongside its theoretical and philosophical side without overwhelming it.
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism

Later, however, Sufism began to turn into a one-sided movement. Physical and mechanical practices gradually came to dominate philosophical reflection. Eventually, these developed into systems, traditions, and purely formal rituals. The Sufi movement then split into different ṭarīqas, or orders, and separate shaykh-led groups, based on little more than these theatrical formalities.
General Conclusions from the Study of Sufism

At that point, the movement finally lost its ideological content. It even turned into a reactionary and parasitic movement that played a dangerous role in numbing society and serving the ideology of reactionary classes.
Why Study Sufism as Part of Philosophy?

I was led to do so because I found in the Sufi intellectual tradition discussions built on philosophical foundations, principles, and concepts. I also found that Sufi theory relied on philosophical ideas when dealing with the two central questions of existence and knowledge.
I therefore came to the conclusion that, in this respect, Sufi thought forms part of Arab-Islamic philosophy. But it is a distinct part, with its own character and its own theory.

There was another reason that convinced me of the importance of studying “Islamic Sufism” from an ideological point of view. When I reread this Sufi intellectual tradition while preparing the material for this book, I became increasingly aware of how closely Engels’s famous words applied to it:

“Throughout the Middle Ages, revolutionary opposition to feudalism continued to appear. Depending on the circumstances of the time, this opposition took the form either of mysticism, of open heresy, or of armed revolt.”

Before writing this chapter, I reread “Islamic Sufism” once again. It seemed to me that Engels, in these words, might almost have been speaking about “revolutionary opposition to feudalism” in the state of the caliphate, and about the very same forms through which this opposition appeared in Arab-Islamic society.
This made me even more certain that my work would be seriously incomplete if I left Sufism out of the study.

After finishing the chapter, rereading it, and comparing it with as many modern studies of “Islamic Sufism” as I could find, I felt the satisfaction of having done something new in this field of thought.
This chapter on Sufism in Islam is divided into two main sections.

The first section deals with Sufism as a form of practical conduct that did not yet depend on a theoretical foundation from outside Islam. This section is limited to the ascetic movement that appeared in the early Islamic period. That movement was influenced by the factional political struggle that broke out at the beginning of Islam among leading Companions of the Prophet over who should hold the caliphate after him.
